newsitem.title: UK: World leaders pay tribute to Deng Xiaoping.
newsitem.headline: World leaders pay tribute to Deng Xiaoping.

text.p: World leaders on Wednesday paid warm tribute to China's late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping for his role in opening up China economically and diplomatically and voiced hopes for a peaceful transition of power in Beijing.
U.S. President Bill Clinton called Deng an "extraordinary figure on the world stage over the past two decades".

In a statement during a visit to Boston, Clinton expressed his sadness at Deng's death late on Wednesday and described him as "the driving force behind China's decision to formalise relations with the United States" in the late 1970s.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, visiting London, paid tribute to Deng and told reporters: "It would obviously be a great advantage to the Chinese as well as to all of us if there were a smooth transition (in Beijing)."
In Taipei, a senior Taiwan official urged Taiwanese people to treat Deng's death calmly, saying the government already has policies for the post-Deng era.

A Funeral Committee formed by the Chinese government shortly after the announcement that Deng, 93, had died in Beijing, said no foreign dignitaries would be invited to the funeral in accordance with the country's practice.
Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said he was greatly saddened by Deng's death, adding "the Japan-China relationship is of growing importance for peace and stability in Asia and the world".

Sir Leon Brittan, European Commissioner with responsibility for relations with Asia, said he expected China to continue along the path of modernisation set out by Deng, who he said had "played a remarkable and courageous role as leader".
French President Jacques Chirac praised the dead Chinese leader as the main force behind his country's modernisation.

"Deng Xiaoping will go down in history as the main architect of the transformations China underwent in the past 20 years and which I was able to measure myself during visits in 1978 and 1991," Chirac said in a message to President Jiang Zemin.

Former U.S. President George Bush praised Deng as a "remarkable leader" who brought benefits to millions of his countrymen by opening up China's economic system. Bush, who was U.S. ambassador to China from 1974 to 1976 and met Deng in China shortly after becoming president in 1989, said he "played a critical role" in establishing strong bilateral ties.
Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten said he had learned with regret of the death of Deng, whom he described as "an historic figure".

"He will be regarded by future generations as an historic figure. His concept of 'one country, two systems' helped to make possible the successful negotiation of the Joint Declaration, and thus to lay the foundation for Hong Kong's stability and prosperity after 1997," Patten said.
Hong Kong will revert to Chinese sovereignty at midnight on June 30, ending more than 150 years of colonial rule.

In London, the office of British Prime Minister John Major expressed regret at the news of Deng's death, adding in a statement that his "initiative played the crucial part in creating today's economically dynamic and successful China."

It said that it was Deng's "visionary concept of one country, two systems'" that facilitated the 1984 Sino-British declaration, guaranteeing Hong Kong's capitalist system would stay in place for 50 years after reversion to Chinese rule.

Xiao Qiang, the leader of Human Rights in China, a prominent New York-based rights group, called on China to free all political prisoners to give the Beijing government "a good start" after Deng's death.
Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien expressed regret over Deng's death but said feelings were mixed because of his record on human rights.

Asked by reporters in Ottawa to comment on Deng's actions in opening China up but also ordering tanks into Tiananmen Square in 1989 to crush pro-democracy demonstrations, Chretien said: "There's always mixed feelings on that situation. That's why whenever we meet with the leaders of China we always mention the rule of law."

The Netherlands, in a brief foreign ministry statement, called Deng a striking personality who engineered a radical transformation of the Chinese economy. It said the "open door policy" pursued by Deng when he came to power in 1978 had resulted in China's dynamic economic development.
The Israeli government expressed sorrow and praised Deng as one of the most outstanding leaders of the century.
